prs.body:
## High Level Overview of Change

This change adds `Scale` to SAV when asset is an IOU, per https://github.com/XRPLF/XRPL-Standards/pull/301

It also removes empty `MPToken` for vault shares when `VaultClawback` or `VaultWithdraw` zeroes the holders shares balance.



### Context of Change

SAV shares are always expressed as an integer, since they are MPTs. We need to ensure that this loss of precision does not cause problems when asset has fractional part, like IOUs do.

reviewCommentsList.author: shawnxie999
reviewCommentsList.body: What soeDEFAULT does is that when sfScale is read like vault->at(sfScale), it will return a default value of zero if the field doesn't exist. In the our case, we are always setting this field, so  soeREQUIRED is more suitable, unless we add a condition like you've suggested.

reviewCommentsList.author: shawnxie999
reviewCommentsList.body:
soeREQUIRED: The field must always be present and must always have an explicit value.

soeDEFAULT; If the field is not actually "present" in the object, then it is assumed to have a default value of zero.  So it's okay to read an soeDEFAULT field that has never been initialized; you'll get back zero.  But you also cannot explicitly initialize an soeDEFAULT field to that default state.

soeOPTIONAL : This field may or may not be present.  If the field is not present, then reading the value produces an exception.

EDIT: this was an explanation from Scott Schurr.

reviewCommentsList.author: shawnxie999
reviewCommentsList.body:
Just want to make sure I understand this correctly. Please let me know if I’m missing something - I’m still pretty new to SAV, so apologies if this is a naive question.

We’re trying to address a precision loss issue when converting an IOU amount (stored as a floating point) into an MPT amount (stored as an integer). Currently, during `STAmount::canonicalize`, if the asset type is MPT(in the case of vault, it is always MPT), the conversion forces the exponent down to 0 by dividing repeatedly, which results in losing decimal places.

To fix this, we’re introducing an Scale, which shifts the decimal point by increasing the exponent during `STAmount` construction, so fractional IOU amounts can be represented as whole integers in MPT amounts. Ideally, the deposited amounts should have fewer decimal places than the scale.


From the spec, it says 

>`Example: With an AssetScale of 6, a deposit of 20.3 assets is correctly converted to 20,300,000 shares (20.3 * 10^6).`

Does this also mean that in JSON we’ll actually show 20,300,000? Would that be confusing to users since it no longer looks like 20.3? My assumption is that users won’t care about the exact number, as long as the conversion is consistent and the balance is correct.

reviewCommentsList.author: Bronek
reviewCommentsList.body: I don't think that would be better. We can also throw in the computation where we calculate shares from assets. In principle we could perform identical computations in `preclaim` and in `doApply` but this seems like unnecessary duplication - and even if factored out, I do not like the complexity it would create.

reviewCommentsList.author: Bronek
reviewCommentsList.body: Yes, the representation of transaction metadata (e.g. transfer of shares in `VaultDeposit`) will have the scale applied, and in this specific example it would be indeed `20300000` shares moved to the depositor.

reviewCommentsList.author: Bronek
reviewCommentsList.body:
the assignment to `shares` would perform rounding to nearest and we do not want that in two cases
- calculation of assets to take from the depositor in `VaultDeposit`
- calculation of assets to clawback when the original (rounded) calculation hits `AssetsAvailable` limit

In all cases we first calculate `shares` (which, depending on context would be rounded or truncated - as listed above) and then calculate `assets` to match the `shares`

reviewCommentsList.author: Bronek
reviewCommentsList.body: If we are given an A (number of assets) then we _always_ (i.e. in `VaultDeposit` `VaultClawback` `VaultWithdraw`) do _roundtrip_ _calculation_ : first from assets to shares, then from such rounded shares to assets again. This guarantees that the number of assets _always_ corresponds with the number of shares, bar rounding of assets (for MPT or XRP) which can go either way. This is similar how DEX works when one side is XRP - which also can go either way due to rounding. If the asset is an IOU then there is no rounding of assets (other than epsilon) which is also similar to how DEX works.
